Notorious means widely known for something bad.

That's the heart of it. Two things must be true at the same time:

  1. Many people know about it (it has fame, a reputation)
  2. What they know is negative (a crime, a flaw, a scandal, a bad habit, a dangerous quality)

If either part is missing, the word doesn't fit. Someone unknown cannot be notorious. And someone known only for good things cannot be notorious either.

Think of "notorious" as fame gone dark. It's what happens when someone or something becomes well-known, but for all the wrong reasons.

A celebrated chef is famous for great food. A notorious chef would be famous for poisoning customers. A famous politician is known for great leadership. A notorious politician is known for corruption and lies.

The fame is real. The knowledge is widespread. But the reason for that fame is the problem.

This is the most important thing to understand: notorious always carries a negative meaning. It is never a neutral or positive word.

You cannot correctly say, "She is notorious for her kindness," or "He is notorious for his generosity," because kindness and generosity are good things. The word would be wrong there. You'd use famous or celebrated instead.

The negative quality baked into "notorious" is what makes it powerful and specific. When you hear it, you immediately know: this person or thing has a bad reputation, and that reputation is well-established and widely spread.
How Serious Does the "Bad Thing" Have to Be?

This is a useful nuance: notorious covers a wide range of severity.

On the serious end, it describes genuinely dangerous or morally wrong things:

  • A notorious serial killer
  • A notorious crime boss
  • A notorious dictator
  • A city notorious for violent crime

On the lighter, more informal end, it can describe milder, even slightly humorous flaws or habits — things that are annoying or funny rather than truly evil:

  • "He is notorious for arriving late to every meeting."
  • "She is notorious for spoiling the ending of movies."
  • "This road is notorious for terrible traffic."

Here, being late or spoiling movies isn't a crime. But the word still fits because the reputation is negative and widely recognized among the people who know the person. In these lighter cases, "notorious" often carries a slightly joking or exasperated tone.

The key is that the word scales naturally. Whether the "bad thing" is as serious as murder or as mild as chronic lateness, notorious works — as long as the negative reputation is real and known.
Who or What Can Be Notorious?

Almost anything can be notorious. The word is not limited to people. Here are the main categories:

People — criminals, corrupt officials, ruthless leaders, dishonest businesspeople:
"Al Capone was a notorious gangster in Chicago."

Places — dangerous areas, crime hotspots, locations associated with terrible events:
"The prison was notorious for its inhumane conditions."

Things — bad policies, scandalous events, faulty products, terrible decisions:
"The company's notorious data breach affected millions of users."

Behaviors or habits — repeated negative patterns:
"The department is notorious for losing important documents."

Here are clear, varied examples to make the meaning stick:

  • "The neighborhood was notorious for drug trafficking and gang violence."
  • "She became notorious after the scandal was reported on national television."
  • "That brand is notorious for making promises it never keeps."
  • "He is a notorious liar — everyone in town knows not to trust him."
  • "The intersection is notorious for car accidents because of poor visibility."
  • "The professor is notorious among students for giving impossible exams."

Notice how in every single case, the person, place, or thing is well-known, and what it is known for is negative.

You will frequently encounter notoriously, which is just the adverb version of notorious. It modifies adjectives or verbs and means "in a way that is widely known to be bad."

  • "The process is notoriously slow." (Everyone knows it's slow — frustratingly so.)
  • "The exam is notoriously difficult." (It has a widespread reputation for being brutal.)
  • "He is notoriously unreliable." (His unreliability is famous and widely recognized.)

It works the same way as the adjective — always negative, always implying a wide reputation.

Understanding a word fully means knowing how it stands apart from words that look similar.

Famous — widely known, but neutral or positive. A famous actor is admired and celebrated.
Notorious — widely known, but always for something bad. A notorious actor has a scandalous or criminal reputation.

Well-known — purely neutral. It just means many people know about something. No positive or negative judgment at all.
Notorious — never neutral. It always implies the reputation is a bad one.

Infamous — this one is the closest to notorious. Both mean widely known for something bad. The difference is subtle: infamous often implies a stronger moral judgment, a sense of deep shame or historical disgrace. Notorious focuses more on the fact of the widespread bad reputation — almost like a statement of reality. In practice, many people use them interchangeably, and that's generally acceptable.

Think of it this way: a notorious criminal is widely known for crime (a statement of reputation). An infamous act is one that history judges harshly and permanently (a moral verdict). But the line is thin, and both words are firmly negative.
A Quick Test to Know If You're Using It Correctly

Ask yourself two questions before using "notorious":

  1. Is the reputation widely known (not just whispered among a small group)?
  2. Is the reputation negative (a flaw, crime, scandal, or bad quality)?

If both answers are yes, "notorious" fits perfectly.
If either answer is no, pick a different word.
The Overall Feeling the Word Creates

When you call something or someone notorious, you are not being neutral. You are making a clear, loaded statement: this thing has earned a dark kind of fame. The word carries weight and implies that the bad reputation is well-deserved, widely acknowledged, and impossible to ignore. It doesn't whisper — it announces.

That is what makes "notorious" such a strong and precise word.
